content: The qualitative study investigated the peer-led manual wheelchair training program known as Wheelchair Self-Efficacy Enhanced for Use (Wheel-See U). This program was the primary intervention explored in the study. In the comparison or control groups across all studies, interventions included standard or usual care (with no specific details provided), waitlist controls, health promotion education sessions, conventional training, typical rehabilitation, or in-person training (if web-based training was being evaluated). The outcomes of these studies were measured using various tools, including different versions of the Wheelchair Skills Test (WST), Life Space Assessment (LSA), Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM), Goal Attainment Score (GAS), and different versions of the Transfer Assessment Instrument (TAI). Other wheelchair skill performance tests assessed abilities such as performing a wheelie or completing specific tasks while using a wheelchair. One study measured wheelchair maintenance capacity and performance using the Wheelchair Maintenance Training Questionnaire (WMT-Q), which evaluated the ability to complete tasks (capacity) and the frequency of task completion (performance). All studies, except one, were conducted among wheelchair users. The exception was a study by Sakakibara et al. (2013), which focused on older adults who might require wheelchair access. Five randomized controlled trials (RCTs) utilized multiple measures of mobility, posture, and functional outcomes. For example, Geisbrecht & Miller (2019) used WST and LSA, Kirby et al. (2015b) used WST, GAS, and LSA, and Miller (2019) used WST and LSA. Van Der Scheer et al. (2016) assessed the ability to perform wheelchair tasks, while Worobey (2016) used WST and GAS. For meta-analysis, the WST was preferred as the primary measure. If WST was unavailable, the next best measure aligned with its construct was chosen. Meta-analysis was feasible for 15 of the 17 RCTs using WST, TAI, and wheelchair task performance measures, comparing wheelchair task training to control groups. These results were based on post-training measurements conducted from immediately after training up to eight weeks. Two RCTs lacked data for statistical pooling, one focusing on wheelchair maintenance training and the other comparing in-person, web-based, and control groups. Worobey et al. (2018) reported significant improvements in wheelchair maintenance activities post-training for both manual and powered wheelchair users, with capacity and performance scores increasing by 36% and 35% for manual users and 89% and 85% for powered users, respectively. Thirteen other experimental studies (12 pre-post and one quasi-experimental) reported on mobility, posture, and functional outcomes across various populations using manual and powered wheelchairs. Eight of the 12 pre-post studies showed significant improvements, while three reported no change, and one had inconsistent findings. The quasi-experimental study also reported significant improvements in inexperienced child wheelchair drivers with disabilities after training. Two cohort studies (one retrospective and one prospective) reported significant improvements in mobility, posture, and functional outcomes among individuals with spinal cord injuries (SCI) after training. Two cross-sectional studies reported inconsistent findings, with one study finding no difference between training protocols and another reporting higher obstacle course scores in the training group compared to the control group. Seven case studies reported on mobility, posture, and functional outcomes, with five showing significant improvements and two reporting inconsistent results. Four case reports also found significant improvements in mobility, posture, and functional outcomes. Satisfaction with wheelchair training was explored in two experimental studies (one pre-post and one quasi-experimental). Participants with disabilities using manual wheelchairs reported greater satisfaction with new wheelchairs compared to their previous ones, particularly in terms of adjustability, safety, durability, ease of use, and comfort. However, no differences were observed between training and comparison groups over time regarding wheelchair comfort among older adults using manual wheelchairs. One RCT used a post-training questionnaire to measure satisfaction, finding that 92% of participants found the training useful and reported improved wheelchair skills, while 100% would recommend the training to others. Participants appreciated the challenge of learning new skills, the quality of trainers, and specific skills taught during the program. Six other experimental studies (five pre-post and one quasi-experimental) reported on empowerment and self-esteem outcomes. Three pre-post studies found significant improvements, while one study had inconsistent findings, and another found no change. The quasi-experimental study reported no differences between groups in empowerment and self-esteem outcomes. Inclusion, participation, and quality of life outcomes were measured using tools such as the Wheelchair Outcome Measure (WhOM), Craig Handicap Assessment and Reporting Technique (CHART), Psychosocial Impact of Assistive Devices Scale (PIADS), Health Utility Index (HUI) Mark 3, and Late Life Function and Disability Index (LLFDI). Two RCTs used multiple measures, with WhOM preferred for meta-analysis. However, data from HUI Mark 3 were used when WhOM data were unavailable. Meta-analysis was feasible for all RCTs, with results based on post-training measurements conducted from five to seven days up to six weeks after training. Three pre-post studies and two cohort studies also reported on inclusion, participation, and quality of life outcomes, with inconsistent findings across constructs and subscales. Three case studies reported on inclusion, participation, and quality of life outcomes for children with disabilities, with two showing improvements. Ongoing follow-up was recommended as an integral part of wheelchair service delivery to address and resolve problems, optimize health and mobility, and prevent harm to wheelchair users. However, the optimal frequency and methods for follow-up remain unknown.
